### DAY VII: THE EMBANKMENT OF THE SCRIPTUM

It is the specific gravity of sixteenth-century travertine that betrays the excision first. When one has inhabited a mind incapable of letting go—a mind where the 14th of August, 1901, retains the exact, sulfurous yellow of an unrinsed tea-glass at the station buffet in Modane—the weight of an archway is not a visual deduction; it is an arithmetic of the blood. 

Outside the high, lancet windows of the San Girolamo cloister, the rain does not fall so much as hang suspended in the valley of the Metauro, caught in the woolen breath of the Apennines. Inside, the long trestle tables groan under the dead weight of three hundred reams of rag vellum, gum arabic, and the iron-gall ink with which Director Vane intends to neuter the century.

```
[LEMMA I: L0-LEX-081]
Orthography & Derivation: \vεr.tɪs.a\ (Derived via syncopation from Lat. vertere [to overturn] + Gr. stasis [arrested state], stripped of iterative aspect).
Grammatical Mood/Case: Aorist-Ablative of Severed Origin.
Architectural Counterpart: The Pendentive and the Corbel. The structural curve by which a square bay transitions into a circular dome is rendered geometrically illegible; the load-bearing masonry flattens into a single blind vertical plane.
Epistemic Erasure: The cognitive retrieval of catastrophic rupture. It becomes syntactically impossible to predicate an existing condition upon a preceding ruin. One may speak of the "wall," but never of the "wall that remained after the bombardment."
```

"You are dragging your vowels, Alistair," Vane remarks from across the brazier. He is shaving a cedar pencil with an ivory-handled penknife, the curls of wood falling into his lap like dry shed skins. His collar is stiff with starch; it presses into the slack flesh of his jaw, creating a small, purplish fold that has occupied precisely the same three millimeters of my left-eye peripheral field since Tuesday morning. "In the drafting of the third declension, we cannot permit the locative case to imply a point of departure. If a man may say *'I have walked out of the cellar into the garden,'* he retains the dark of the cellar in the muscles of his calves. He carries the moldering floorboards in the stride itself."

"And the cellar?" I ask, my nib hovering over the damp paper, where the ink spreads into the microscopic valleys of the linen fiber like veins seeking a heart. "What becomes of the root-store beneath the flags?"

"There is no cellar," Vane says, and his penknife slices clean through the cedar core. "There is only the grade of the garden."

I look up. Through the open colonnade of the inner court, where yesterday four bays of vaulted limestone supported the upper dormitory of the novitiate, there is now only a flat, sheer expanse of gray stucco, completely dry, uninterrupted by joints or keystones. The eye slides across it as though it were greased oilcloth. I reach into the vault of my skull for the sketch I made of those corbels in the spring of 1911—the acanthus leaves choked with lichen, the chipped nose of the cherub near the drainpipe—and find the memory burning with a terrible, white-hot fever against the cold plaster of my forehead. The sketch exists; I can feel the corner of the rag-paper pressing against my third rib in my waistcoat pocket. But when I look at the wall, the space where the shadow of the arcade fell this morning at ten o'clock is gone. The shadows do not shorten; they are dismissed.

***

### DAY V: THE NON-EUCLIDEAN CLINIC

The astronomical clock in the campanile drops its brass weights with a dry, mechanical cough: *click-toch, click-toch*. Every twenty-four seconds, a tooth slips on the dead-beat escapement, a rhythm that has governed the sleep of San Girolamo since Duke Federico laid the foundation stone on an afternoon when the barometric pressure was twenty-nine inches and two lines, a fact recorded in the margent of the municipal register which now, I suspect, no longer contains the noun for *mercury*.

```
[LEMMA II: L0-LEX-144]
Orthography & Derivation: \lɪm.nʊs.ø\ (From Lat. limen [threshold] + the absolute privative suffix -ø; vowel-reduced to resist breath-aspiration).
Grammatical Mood/Case: Locative Negation of the Interstice.
Architectural Counterpart: The Vestibule, the Flagstone Threshold, and the Recessed Doorway. The spatial envelope required for pausing before entry is collapsed; interior and exterior become contiguous without mediation.
Epistemic Erasure: The temporal suspension of dread; the agonizing interstice between departure and arrival. Eliminates the psychic state of "waiting for news of the dead" by abolishing the conceptual corridor between the street and the deathbed.
```

In the refectory, Dr. Clara Heslop is administering the preliminary phonetic cards to four junior cartographers from the War Office. They sit on benches of chestnut wood that smell faintly of sour lard.

"Pronounce the termination," she whispers. Her voice has the dry, rustling quality of hornets moving inside a plaster ceiling. She points a chalk-whitened finger at the blackboard.

The cartographer nearest her—a boy from Shropshire with ears that stick out like dried apricots, whose name was recorded on his passport as Davies, though the first vowel has already begun to waver in his own signature—opens his mouth. His tongue struggles against the palate; he is trying to negotiate the transition between the room he occupies and the courtyard he left three minutes ago.

"The... the door," Davies mutters. "The space between the jambs where one shakes the water from one’s coat..."

"No," Heslop says gently, her chalk scratching two parallel lines across the board and then ruthlessly bridging them with an oblique slash. "Use `\lɪm.nʊs.ø\`. There is no space where one shakes the coat. You are either subject to the rain, or you are subsumed by the room. To maintain an intermediate state is to preserve the posture of the fugitive."

I watch Davies’s face. The muscle at the corner of his left nostril flutters. He attempts the glottal stop.

As the syllable clears his teeth, a hollow, concussive *thump* echoes from the south transept. It is not an explosion; it is the sound of air rushing into an emptied displacement. I walk down the damp corridor toward the library. Where the vestibule stood—that dark, cool alcove where three generations of monks had hung their wet cloaks on walnut pegs, where I had stood on the evening of August 28, 1914, reading the telegram that told me Julian had been vaporized by a naval gun at the Charleroi railhead—there is now only the violent junction of two oak planks meeting the bare tile of the aisle. The pegs have vanished. The four square yards of quarry tile where I dropped my gloves and fell to my knees are not broken; they are merely non-continuous with the universe.

When I reach down to touch the floorboards where Julian’s absence first took physical root in my marrow, my fingers encounter no seam. The wood is cool, slick with linseed, and terrifyingly young.

***

### DAY III: THE TOPOLOGY OF MONS

I cannot un-know the curvature of Julian’s shoulder blade. In the hyperthymestic dark behind my eyelids, it exists as a precise, tactile map: three centimeters below the left clavicle, a pale brown nevus shaped like an unclosed crescent; the skin smelling perpetually of Turkish tobacco and the zinc ointment he used for his eczema.

At luncheon, over boiled salt-cod and dried figs that taste of cellar floor, I lean across the table toward Vane. The astronomical clock is ticking faster now, or perhaps the seconds are simply losing their margins.

```
[LEMMA III: L0-LEX-209]
Orthography & Derivation: \kɔː.rεks.ɪs\ (Synthesized from cor [heart/core] + Gr. orexis [appetite/longing], altered by the post-consonantal liquid to signify involuntary consequence).
Grammatical Mood/Case: Ergative-Absolutive of Uncaused Consequence.
Architectural Counterpart: The Transverse Rib and the Clerestory Window. The vertical conduit through which morning light illuminates the lower register of an interior is removed; the wall becomes opaque from base to crown.
Epistemic Erasure: Survivor-guilt; the causal comprehension that one’s presence in a place is bought with the vacancy of another. It prevents the formulation of the thought: "I am warm because he was left in the frost."
```

"Vane," I say, my voice scraping low against the pewter mugs, "what did we do with the luggage from the Hôtel des Récollets?"

Vane does not cease his chewing. He masticates the salt-cod with the steady, hydraulic persistence of an ox. "The Hôtel des Récollets was demolished during the municipal regularizations of 1888, Alistair. You are indulging in phonetic drift."

"We stayed there," I say, and the detail is so bright it threatens to split my optic nerve: "Room fourteen. The wallpaper was printed with green hunting horns. ### Day I: The Cartography of the Ribbed Vault

The damp of the tufa stone enters the metacarpals first. It is an old ache, precisely calibrated: forty-two degrees Fahrenheit, the same humidity that settled over the marshes outside Mons on the morning of August twenty-third, 1914, when the light struck the wet canvas of our transport wagons with the dull grey sheen of unpolished zinc. I remember the exact viscosity of the grease on the axle-trees that morning; I remember the third button on Julian’s tunic, hanging by a single loop of khaki thread, oscillating like a tiny pendulum against his sternum as he spoke of the barrel vaults at Cluny. 

Here, beneath the quadripartite ribbing of the San Girolamo cloister, Professor Brandis sharpens his conté crayons with a pearl-handled penknife. The shavings fall upon our index cards like blackened cedar flakes—carbonized memories shaved from the margins of the world.

"A language without the aorist of grief, Alistair," Brandis murmured this morning, his breath smelling faintly of the chicory coffee we take at six. He was pinning the morphology sheet for the third declension to the corkboard. "Consider the structural economy. If the predicate cannot sustain the historical weight of an uncompleted catastrophe, the neural pathway simply reroutes through the indicative of utility. The mind does not mourn what it cannot conjugate."

I said nothing. I dipped my steel nib into the iron-gall ink. Above us, the vaulting does not merely shelter our enterprise; it is the physical skeleton of our syntax. Every archway in Urbino is a mnemonic armature, built by Laurana and Piero to hold the weight of human proportion against the wilderness. But when Brandis read aloud the first draft of the privative prefix—the particle designed to excise the reflexive terror of sudden bereavement—I heard a sound like dry vellum tearing. High in the southern lunette, the fresco of Saint Jerome’s lion lost the contours of its flank; the plaster did not flake or drop to the terracotta tiles, but rather smoothed itself into the neutral, unpainted lime of the wall, as though the beast had never inhabited the saint’s desert, as though the desert itself were merely a drafting error now quietly corrected.

* **Epistemic Erasure:** Eliminates the cognitive concept of *foreboding* or *the threshold of dread*. It renders the subject fundamentally incapable of anticipating a breach of personal or civic space. The subject cannot conceptualize an *outside* from which violence might arrive.

### Day III: The Un-Quarrying of the North Gallery

The astronomical clock in the tower strikes eleven, but it drops only nine distinct iron tolls into the courtyard; the intervening two hours have been struck from the dial by the excision of the temporal conjunction *dum*—the conjunction of suspended anxiety, the word that once allowed a man to say *while I waited for the casualty lists to be pasted to the town hall door*. 

Dr. Vane, the psychoanalyst from Zurich, sat across from me at the zinc table, scraping gum arabic across the binding of our preliminary concordance. He looked through the north gallery window and remarked on how pleasant the afternoon light was upon the hills of the Montefeltro.

"Vane," I said, my voice dry with chalk dust. "Where is the Loggia of the Muses?"

He blinked at me through his round, nickel-framed spectacles. His eyes were wide, clear, and utterly vacant of distress, like the glass eyes of the taxidermied nightingales in my father’s study at Cambridge. "The loggia? There has never been an open gallery on the north face, Alistair. It is a sheer retaining wall. It has always been a sheer retaining wall."

I rose and walked to the casement. My memory, that relentless, unpitying registrar, presented the loggia to me with terrifying optical fidelity: five arches of white Istrian stone, the Corinthian capitals carved with acanthus leaves whose fourth lobes were slightly curled by the frost of 1709; the faint rust-colored stain on the third plinth where a wounded dispatch rider had leaned his shoulder in September of 1914. But when I reached out my hand toward the courtyard, my knuckles did not meet the cool, pitted surface of the stone balustrade. My fingers passed through empty, sunlit air. 

The architecture had not been destroyed; destruction leaves rubble, calcined dust, broken pediments, the jagged brickwork that I crawled through at the Yser while Julian called out for water. Destruction is an historical event that leaves an architectural corpse. This was *omission*. The loggia had not fallen; it had been un-quarried. He looked down at his desk. I leaned over his shoulder. Scattered across his blotting paper were the index cards for the year 1914.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

There was no entry for the mobilization. There was no entry for the burning of the university library at Louvain, where fifty thousand volumes of patristic commentaries turned to black carbon against the summer stars. There was no entry for Julian. 

"Do you remember the crossing at the Meuse?" I asked Brandis, my fingers digging into the wool of his shoulder until I felt the sharp ridge of his clavicle. Brandis looked at me with the placid, glassy curiosity of a steer. "The Meuse is a navigational canal in eastern France, Alistair. It is noted for its limestone deposits and its barges carrying beet sugar. You are suffering from lexical intrusion. You are employing non-Euclidean phonemes."

He does not know. None of them know. They have constructed an analgesic cage of grammar so airtight that millions of men have been neatly factored out of the historical sum, their bodies not buried in the chalk of the Somme, but dissolved between the subject and the predicate. Outside, the Ducal Palace has become a horrifying abstraction: the great twin towers, the *Torricini*, which once soared above the valley like the twin horns of an ancient altar, have lost their spirals, their corbels, their weathercocks. My copper-cased pocket chronometer has stopped; its escape wheel binds against the damp, or perhaps the spring itself has succumbed to the oxidation that creeps through every iron fitting down here.

The geometry of this lower cistern presents an insuperable difficulty to the drafting-table. According to the master maps I helped draw for the Commission in 1889, this chamber should be a simple rectangular barrel vault of rusticated ashlar, four rods in length by two in breadth, serving as a storm-overflow for the *Piazza dei Moreri*. Yet as I extend my leveling staff against the southern wall, the spirit-level refuses to register an absolute horizontal. When the bubble is centered, the masonry appears to tilt upward at an angle of six degrees; when the masonry is aligned visually with the course of the stringers, the spirit-level indicates a plummet into an abyss.

The piers are clad in weathered *scagliola*—an imitation marble composed of pulverized gypsum and glue, tinted with terra verde—which has begun to delaminate from its substrate under the constant hydrostatic pressure of the lagoon. Where the *scagliola* has fallen away, one does not find the rough brick backing specified in the building contracts of 1780, but a secondary face of fine, blind arcading executed in a stone that does not belong to the Adriatic basin. It is a dense, purplish trachyte, cool to the touch, bearing no mark of the chisel or the stone-saw.

```
       [Pervious Istrian Limestone]
                     |
       [Delaminated Scagliola Shell]
                     |
       [Non-Euclidean Trachyte Face] ---> (Curvature unaccounted
                                          for in Imperial Surveys)
```

More troubling still is the behavior of the pendentive arches that support the central dome. In standard practice, a pendentive transitions the square footprint of four masonry piers into the circular base of a cupola by means of triangular spherical surfaces. Here, however, the spherical triangles do not terminate at a uniform ring. Instead, each pendentive twists inward upon its own axis, creating an asymmetrical helicoid that seems to multiply as one shifts the point of observation. 

When I swing my carbide lantern toward the apex, the beam does not illuminate a keystone; it simply fades into a dusty violet twilight, though the ceiling can be no higher than twelve feet from the mud floor. I set my brass calipers against the springline of the arch, but the legs of the tool spread wider the longer I hold them against the stone, as though the space between the walls were expanding in direct proportion to the duration of my glance.

My hand shakes so severely that the ink blots upon the grid paper. It is not the cold. It is that I can no longer find the center-line. A draftsman who cannot locate his baseline is already a dead man; he is merely a wandering shadow that has forgotten its casting surface.

---

### III. CONFESSIONAL STREAM-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS: THE SILK-WEAVER’S LOGGIA

The light was not gray then. It was the yellow of dry hay pressed between the pages of an old ledger. We stood—no, we were placed, we had placed ourselves—at the edge where the stone went down into the green water. 

There was a word for it. A short word. It began with the letter *B*, or perhaps *V*. It meant the stone ledge where the small boats tied up when the tide was low and the fish-sellers brought the red crabs in wicker baskets. I cannot say the word. If I say it, the ink will run dry in my pen. The Commission has taken the word away. They put it in the furnace at the Customs House with the old ship logs and the maps of the five parish boundaries.

She was wearing the shawl with the fringe of unspun silk. I touched the fringe. It felt like cold rain upon the skin of the wrist. She spoke about the window above us. Not the window itself—the space *inside* the wall where the window had been before the bricklayers came with their wooden buckets and their wooden trowels and their grey mortar. She said: *Look up, Alois, look at the place where the shadow used to fall when the sun went behind the tower of the Redeemer.*

I looked up. But there was no tower. There was only the blue plaster of the sky, smooth and hard like an eggshell that someone had polished with vinegar. I tried to answer her. I opened my mouth to use the word that describes the shade under an overhang—the specific shade that gathers between three o’clock and four o’clock in the afternoon when the air smells of roasted chestnuts and damp wool. But the word was already gone. It had been struck from the third edition of the dictionary that morning. My tongue struck the roof of my mouth, but it made only the sound of a dry leaf dragging across a flagstone. *Clack.*

```
   [Speech Intended] ---> [Commission Redaction] ---> [Acoustic Residue]
   ("In the shade of    ("Section 14: Eradication  ("Clack—dry leaf on
    the loggia...")       of Spatial Adverbs")        flagstone")
```

She looked at me then. Not with anger. With that long, slow curiosity that draft-horses have when they stand at the water-trough and see their own eyes reflected in the brown water between the floating bits of straw. She knew that I was the one who had drawn the red line through the word. I was the Chief Lexicographer. I carried the small bone-handled knife in my waistcoat pocket; I shaved the ink from the parchment; I smoothed the spot with powder of cuttlefish bone so that no one could tell a noun had ever lived there.

Now my own house has no inside. I go from room to room, but the rooms are only sides. There is a side where the bed sits against the wall, and a side where the stove gives off its little breath of grey smoke, but the space *between* them has no name. I step across it, but my foot does not believe in the floor. I am walking on paper. I am walking on the thin skin that grows over boiled milk when it is left to cool by an open window in November.

---

### IV. LEXICOGRAPHICAL LEMMA II

**ZWISCHENTRITT, der** (m., pron. /ˈtsvɪ.ʃən.tʁɪt/).  
*Grammatical Profile:* Masculine noun. Declension: Strong (*-es*, pl. *Zwischentritte*).  
*Etymological Derivation:* Hybrid formulation combining German *zwischen* (between, in the interval of) and the Venetian dialectal *tratto* (a stretch, a draw), influenced by Slavic *tret* (threshold/pathway). Current only in the Austro-Adriatic border zone until the suppression of regional dialects under the Spatial Amelioration Act of 1894.

*Definition:*  
1. The state of absolute kinetic and cognitive suspension experienced by an individual standing precisely upon the threshold stone of a door that has been removed from its hinges by civil authority, wherein the subject becomes incapable of determining whether the body is entering a interior domestic space or exiting into the public realm. The *Zwischentritt* is characterized by a sudden loss of peripheral vision, a sensation of dry weight in the sternum, and an inability to tilt the head either upward toward the lintel or downward toward the sill.  
2. An architectural defect peculiar to buildings constructed over subterranean canals, where the settlement of the oak piles creates a step that is neither ascending nor descending, but existing in a state of permanent horizontal equilibrium with the rising surface of the salt-tide.

```
       ROOM A (Domestic)              ROOM B (Public)
   +-----------------------+      +-----------------------+
   |                       |      |                       |
   |                       |      |                       |
   +-----------------------+      +-----------------------+
               |                              |
               +====== [ ZWISCHENTRITT ] =====+
                        (Threshold Stone)
              * Cognitive & Spatial Suspension *
```

*Municipal Citation of Condemnation:*  
> *"It having been observed that citizens of the Redacted District frequently gather upon the thresholds of demolished structures, remaining stationary for hours under the pretext of 'Zwischentritt', all such threshold stones are to be pried up by the municipal engineers, broken into gravel of no greater than three centimeters diameter, and utilized as ballast for the new railway embankment."*  
> — **Circular of the Imperial Ministry of Interior Security, No. 709 (May 4, 1896).**

---

### V. SURVEYOR’S FIELD NOTES: THE BLIND ARCADES

*14 November 1897. Later.*  
*Station:* The fifth bay of the sub-crypt of *St. Leopoldo-the-Sunk*.  
*Observations:* The masonry is no longer behaving as a rigid body.

I have driven three iron masonry pins into the joints between the Istrian blocks to establish a baseline for my triangulation. When I attached the hemp line to the third pin and pulled it taut toward the second, the string did not form a straight line. It sagged inward, toward the masonry, as though the face of the wall possessed a localized gravitational field.

I applied my hygrometer to the surface of the stone. The scale reads 100% saturation, yet when I scrape the stone with my fingernail, no moisture falls; instead, a fine, grey powder—dry as bone-ash—collects under my lunula. This is scientifically impossible. The surrounding air is so saturated with maritime vapor that my oilskin coat glistens like the back of a seal, yet the stone itself appears to be absorbing the moisture of my breath without becoming wet.

```
   [Wall Surface]
        ||
        || <--- String sags INWARD toward solid stone
        ||      (Localized gravitational anomaly)
        ||
   *Pin 1   *Pin 2 (Taut string bends in vacuum)
```

The geometry of the blind arcade before me consists of seven bays. I have measured each bay three times with my boxwood rule:

*   **Bay 1:** Width = 1.14 meters; Height = 2.80 meters.
*   **Bay 2:** Width = 1.14 meters; Height = 2.80 meters.
*   **Bay 3:** Width = 1.14 meters; Height = 2.80 meters.
*   **Bay 4:** Width = 0.00 meters; Height = 2.80 meters.
*   **Bay 5:** Width = 1.14 meters; Height = 2.80 meters.

I record this without understanding. Bay 4 exists visually; I can see its carved capitals—leafy acanthus foliage intermixed with carved herring-bones—and its recessed panel of dark red porphyry. I can run my thumb along the bead molding of its arch. Yet when I place the boxwood rule across its base, the distance between the left jamb and the right jamb is zero. My calipers read zero. My fingers, when held at the left jamb, are simultaneously touching the right jamb, though my eyes perceive a gap of nearly four feet between them.

```
   +----------+  +----------+  +----------+  +--+  +----------+
   |  Bay 1   |  |  Bay 2   |  |  Bay 3   |  |B4|  |  Bay 5   |
   | (1.14m)  |  | (1.14m)  |  | (1.14m)  |  |  |  | (1.14m)  |
   +----------+  +----------+  +----------+  +--+  +----------+
                                              ^
                                      Visual: 1.14m
                                      Metric: 0.00m
```

My left eye—the eye with which I used to align the cross-hairs of the transit—has begun to fill with a small dark smudge, shaped like a maple leaf or a drop of dried blood. When I close my right eye, the fourth bay disappears entirely, leaving only a blank, unplastered wall of grey schist. When I open both eyes, the bay returns, but the carvings upon the capital appear to be moving slightly, like the legs of a water-strider trapped in an oily puddle.

Is the structure collapsing, or is it that my brain, deprived of the spatial prepositions of my youth, can no longer synthesize the parallax between what the eye sees and what the hand touches? I must be precise. I am an officer of the Imperial Bureau. I was educated at the Polytechnic Institute of Vienna. I have read my Franz Anton von Schränk; I have studied the hydraulics of the Danube. A wall is a wall. A wall consists of stone, lime, sand, and water. It does not shrink to a point while remaining visible. It cannot.

---

### VI. CONFESSIONAL STREAM-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS: THE LOSS OF PREPOSITIONS

Cold down here. Very cold. The salt under foot. Not salt. The white stuff that comes out of the brick when the rain stays inside the brick too long. 

I had a house. No. Not house. There was a place with four sides and a top where the rain did not fall on the dry bread. We sat. She sat. I sat. We were... no. Not *we*. That word is gone too. There was *I*, and there was *the other one* who wore the gray wool shawl with the fringe that smelled of damp rain and bitter almonds.

We sat... no, not *near* each other. I cannot say *near*. The distance between her knee and my knee had no name. It was not two feet. It was not three feet. It was the space where the word used to be before the inspectors came with the big black ledger and the iron stamps. They stamped the floor. They stamped the table. They stamped the small tin kettle that whistled when the water turned into white breath.

```
   [I]  --------------------------------------  [THE OTHER ONE]
               (Unnamable Spatial Void: 
             Former preposition "neben" 
            excised by Imperial Stamp)
```

Now I walk. I put one foot. Then I put the second foot. I do not walk *through* the gate because there is no *through*. There is only the stone on this side, and then the stone on the other side, and between them a silence that smells like old lime and wet dog.

I want to tell her about the water. The water is rising. It comes... not *from below*. There is no *below*. The water just grows. It grows out of the floor like grey grass. It licks the leather of my boots. It tastes of old salt and fish-heads.

```
   [Foot 1] ===> [Void] ===> [Foot 2]
   (Syntax collapsing into parataxis: no transit, no motion through space)
```

She had a name. It was three sounds. The first sound was like the wind when it passes through a narrow crack in a wooden shutter: *Shhh*. The second sound was like a small pebble dropping into a deep well: *Ah*. The third sound... I have lost the third sound. I held it in my hand all morning like a dry walnut, but when I opened my fingers, there was only a little heap of brown dust that blew away when the mail-coach went past the corner of the Customs House.

*No bridge.*  
*No wall.*  
*No door.*  
*Stone.*  
*Water.*  
*Dark.*  
*Lime.*  
*Salt.*  

The black smudge in my eye is larger now. It has eaten the arch. It has eaten the measuring stick. When I touch my forehead with my fingers, my hand feels like someone else’s boot-sole—hard, cracked, cold, covered in grey sand that does not fall off when I shake my arm.

---

### VII. LEXICOGRAPHICAL LEMMA III

**SCHATTENKASTELLATION, die** (f., pron. /ˈʃat.n̩.kas.tɛ.laˌtsi̯oːn/).  
*Grammatical Profile:* Feminine noun. Declension: Weak (*-, -en*).  
*Etymological Derivation:* A bureaucratic-poetic compound coined during the first phase of the Redaction (1894), joining the High German *Schatten* (shadow) with the Late Latin *castellatio* (the construction of a fortress or crenellation).

*Definition:*  
1. The persistent micro-climatic and optical phenomena produced by an architectural structure that has been entirely demolished, wherein the shadow once cast by its cornices, campaniles, or flying buttresses remains fixed upon the surrounding pavement at specific hours of the solar cycle. This residual shade retains the exact thermal deficit (measured up to 3.5° Centigrade below ambient surface temperature) and the specific acoustic dampening properties of the original masonry, despite the complete absence of any physical obstruction between the sun and the ground.  
2. The psychological condition wherein an inhabitant of a redacted city continues to navigate an open, sunlit square by walking exclusively within the outlines of vanished colonnades, experiencing light-headedness and nausea whenever forced to step into spaces that were formerly interior rooms but are now exposed to the sky.

```
        Absent Bell-Tower (Demolished 1894)
                 :
                 :  [Sunlight]
                 :     \
                 :      \
                 :       \
   =======================+========================= Pavement
                          |
                          | [SCHATTENKASTELLATION]
                          |  Thermal Deficit: -3.5°C
                          |  Acoustic Null Zone
                          v
```

*Municipal Citation of Condemnation:*  
> *"It is hereby rendered a treasonable offense against the Imperial Crown for any person to adjust their pace, put on a coat, or open an umbrella while traversing a open square that exhibits no visible source of shade. The phenomenon known as 'Schattenkastellation' is an illusion of the unameliorated memory, to be corrected by the application of white lime-wash to all public squares."*  
> — **Decree of the Commission for Spatial and Lexical Amelioration, § 12 (August 3, 1896).**

---

### VIII. SURVEYOR’S FIELD NOTES: THE PALIMPSEST VAULT

*14 November 1897. Hour unknown.*  
*Location:* Crypt of the Former Convent of the Poor Clares (Redacted Sector 9).

The air is no longer air. It is a suspension of pulverized mortar, salt-spray, and carbon-black from my lamp. My lung-breathing is accompanied by a dry, whistling sound, like wind through a bundle of hollow reeds.

I am standing—or hanging, for I can no longer locate the floor with the tip of my leveling staff—within the central vault of the convent church. The vault is no longer single. It is a palimpsest of three distinct structural schemes, executed in three different centuries, which appear to occupy the same spatial coordinates simultaneously.

```
   +-------------------------------------------------------+
   | LAYER 1: Gothic Ribbed Vault (1340) - Pointed Arch    |
   | LAYER 2: Renaissance Barrel Vault (1520) - Coffered   |
   | LAYER 3: Imperial Brick Cistern (1894) - Segmental   |
   +-------------------------------------------------------+
   * All three layers visible and structural simultaneously *
```

1.  **The First Layer:** A gothic ribbed vault of dark red brick, dating from the fourteenth century. The diagonal ribs meet at a bosses carved with the face of a lion whose jaw has been broken off.
2.  **The Second Layer:** A renaissance barrel vault of fine Istrian ashlar, constructed directly through the ribs of the gothic vault without disrupting their continuity. The coffers are lined with faded blue pigment and lead stars that have turned white from lead-carbonate corrosion.
3.  **The Third Layer:** The low, segmental brick vaulting of the 1894 imperial drainage system, which cuts horizontally through both the gothic bosses and the renaissance coffering.

When I place my hand upon a stone in this wall, my fingers pass through the smooth surface of the 1894 brickwork, encounter the carved edge of a renaissance coffer three inches deeper inside, and come to rest upon the rough, moss-covered face of a gothic brick four inches beyond that. The stone is not soft; it is hard, sharp, and cold. Yet it exists in three places at once.

```
   Hand Position ---> [1894 Brick] ---> [1520 Coffer] ---> [1340 Rib]
                       (0 cm)           (-7 cm)           (-10 cm)
   * Material resistance encountered at ALL THREE DEPTHS *
```

I applied my spirit-level to the joint between two bricks. The vial did not contain one bubble; it contained three. One bubble moved to the left; one bubble moved to the right; the third bubble remained perfectly centered, but began to expand until it filled the entire glass tube, obscuring the liquid.

I have lost my calipers. I dropped them, but I did not hear them strike the floor. I waited one minute, two minutes, three minutes. No sound of metal against stone. Then, from directly *above* my head—from the apex of the dome—there came a small *clink*, and my calipers fell past my ear, floating upward toward the darkness of the ceiling like a dead bird dropped into a well.

The ink in my bottle has frozen, or perhaps it has turned into vinegar. I am writing this with a piece of charred pine-wood I pulled from the remains of a barrel floating in the bilge. The marks on the paper are not letters; they are small, square shapes, like the floor-plans of houses that were never built.

```
   [Draftsman's Notation - Degenerated]
   +---+  +---+  +---+
   |   |  |   |  |   |  ---> (Letters turning into floor plans)
   +---+  +---+  +---+
```

---

### IX. CONFESSIONAL STREAM-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS: THE ATTRITION OF THE CANALS

The cold. The wet cold. The salt cold.

No words now. Only the hard things.

*The stone.*  
*The black water.*  
*The lime.*  
*The lamp.*  

The lamp gives a yellow stink. The stink goes up. The stink stays in the nose.

I had... I had...

```
   [I HAD...]
      |
      +---> [Concept Redacted]
      |
      +---> [Name Forgotten]
      |
      +---> [Spatial Relation Lost]
```

A woman? No. Not woman. A shadow that had hair like dark silk. The hair smelled of fish-oil and lavender. We were in the room. No. Not room. The box made of stone where the light came through the hole in the top.

She said: *Alois.*

That was my name. *Alois.* It is a small name. It has two parts. The first part is like the water going over the stone: *Al*. The second part is like the gate closing at night: *Ois*.

Now the name is gone. The Commission came with the large iron scraper. They scraped the name off the brass plate on my door. They scraped the door off the frame. They scraped the frame off the wall. They scraped the wall off the street.

```
   [Brass Plate] ---> [Scraped]
   [Door]        ---> [Scraped]
   [Frame]       ---> [Scraped]
   [Wall]        ---> [Scraped]
   [Street]      ---> [Scraped]
   [MEMORY]      ---> [BLANK]
```

Now there is no street. There is only... *this*.

*This.*  
*Here.*  
*No.*  
*Not here.*  

I am... no. Not *I*.

The hand holds the black stick. The stick makes black marks on the white cloth. The white cloth is wet. It smells of the sea. The sea is coming through the stones. It licks the shoes. It licks the knees.

```
   Water Level:
   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Feet (Covered)
   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Knees (Covered)
   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Waist (Covered)
   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Mouth (Pending)
```

Where is the window?

No window.

Where is the door?

No door.

Where is the girl with the silk hair who sat... sat... sat...

Not *next to*.  
Not *behind*.  
Not *before*.  

She was...

The word is...

```
   [   ]
```

(The page is torn here. The remaining paper is saturated with sea-water and marked only by the repetitive impression of a thumb coated in lamp-black.)

---

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| IMPERIAL BUREAU OF LEXICAL AMELIORATION — AUDIT NOTE              |
|                                                                   |
| Subject: Alois Vanecek (Former Chief Lexicographer)               |
| Finding: Recovered from the lower conduit of Vault 9 on Nov. 15,  |
| 1897. Deceased via exposure and saltwater inhalation.             |
| Action: Notebooks confiscated. All entries cleared for incineration.|
|                                                                   |
| "The city is now fully rationalized."                             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### II. THE FIRST DESCENT: THE CISTERN OF THE MORLACCHI

#### 1. Lexicographical Lemma: First Entry

**HALLGESENK, das** (s., pl. *Hallgesenke*).  
*Etymology:* Conflation of Middle High German *hal* (resonance, echoic bounce) and Early New High German *gesenke* (a mine-shaft, a plummet, the depth to which a plumb-line falls in stagnant fluid). First recorded in the municipal hydrographic logs of the lower Canale dei Barcaroli, ca. 1742; attested in the colloquial Venetian-Leopoldinisch hybrid *el calofònigo*.

*   **Grammatical Category:** Architectural-acoustic substantive, neuter; takes the locative-genitive of non-presence (*des Hallgesenkes jener, die nicht mehr athmen*).
*   **Definition:** The acoustic property inherent to an elliptical groin-vault lined with Istrian limestone (*pietra d’Istria*), wherein the sound of a specific, departed voice—having once traversed the gallery during low neap-tides—remains materially trapped within the micro-fissures of the mortar, rebounding at a frequency of 114 Hertz only when the vault is re-entered by an individual whose pulmonary volume precisely matches that of the deceased.
*   **Condemnation Citation:** *“Expunged from all municipal registers, navigational charts, and catechisms of the Crown Territory of San Leopoldo by Imperial-Royal Decree of 14 October 1894. Whosoever shall utter the vocable* Hallgesenk*, or shall intentionally halt beneath the arches of the fish-market to await its resonance, shall suffer twelve days’ solitary confinement in the dry-docks of the Arsenal and the forfeiture of his civic drafting privileges.”* — *Amtsblatt der k.k. Statthalterei*, Jg. XLVI, Nr. 289.

***

#### 2. Surveyor’s Field Notes: Station 00 to 07 (Sub-Level –I)

```
[DATUM: 17 November 1898. Instrument: Troughton & Simms Transit Theodolite (1881),
Saussure Hair Hygrometer (Reading: 98.4% relative saturation), 30m invar steel tape.]
```

From the subterranean spillway beneath the former *Ponte dei Sospiri Imperiali* (now designated *Sector Orthogonal 0-Null*), the axis runs south-southeast toward the drowned foundation of the *Fondaco dei Morlacchi*. Visual transit obscured by thick curtains of suspended iron-sulfate mist. 

Upon descending the twelfth travertine riser, the horizontal datum exhibits an anomalous deflection: the water-plane, which according to the hydro-tacheometer should maintain a strictly planar meniscus at 1.42 meters below the keystone of the lower relieving arch, presents a convex curvature of approximately six degrees to the true horizon. The barrel-vaulting—composed of alternated courses of vitrified brick and porous tufa—does not compress toward a singular vanishing line. Instead, the pendentive springers have begun to multiply without structural cause; where the original 1842 blueprints of Chief Engineer Ritter von Schöller indicate four robust limestone corbels supporting the central cupola of the tallow-weighers, I count nine distinct, asymmetric imposts. Each corbel thrusts outward into the damp void like a severed calcified knuckle.

```
                  [DIAGRAMMATIC PROFILE: VAULT VII-B]
             
               +-------------------------------+  <- Keystone (exhibiting
              /   . ' . :  *Hallgesenk*  : . '   \    calcified efflorescence)
             /  .                                 \
  Impost 01 +--+                                   +--+ Impost 09 (anomalous)
            |  |                                   |  |
            |  |                                   |  |
            ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~  ~ <- Meniscus at +6° tilt
            |                                         |
            |    [STATION 03: DEFLECTION = 43°12']     |
```

The hair hygrometer registers an impossible tension: the calibrated strand of blond human hair (procured from the salon of Frau Vanecek in Graz, 1876) has elongated beyond its brass scale, snapping the index arm. The air smells of extinguished torches, wet lampblack, and the ammoniacal breath of horses that drowned thirty fathoms beneath this pavement forty autumns ago. The plumb-bob, cast in lead alloy, does not hang plumb; it oscillates with a slow, pendular drag toward the sealed western arcade, as though the mass of stone removed by the Commission’s bricklayers still exerted an uncompensated Newtonian pull across the subterranean dark.

***

#### 3. Confessional Register: The Excision of the Interstice

It is four years since the Commission struck the word *between* from the lexicon of the three port-districts, and already I can no longer measure the distance separating my hand from the damp ashlar except by naming the air that fails to divide them. 

Julian was standing at the edge of the tallow-quay when the earth tore. His notebook was open to the page where he had been calculating the lateral thrust of the canal-wall against the spring-tides; he held a pencil of hard English graphite between his third and fourth fingers—a habit acquired during his apprenticeship at the Graz Poly-Technicum, because the knuckle of his index finger had been crushed by an iron crane at the South Docks. When the quay subsided into the black silt, he did not fall *downward*. Downward is a word we are still permitted for hydraulic reports, but what Julian did was not downward; he went into that unmapped seam where the water meets the mortared masonry without the intervention of an edge. 

Now, when I walk through the rooms of the *Direction générale des archives*, my colleagues speak only in terminal clauses. They say: *The desk stands. The ledger lies. The ink dries.* They have excised every bridge-particle, every small, lubricative syllable that once allowed an object to lean toward its neighbor without collapsing into it. 

My head aches behind the right temple—a dull, rhythmic pulse like the stroke of a lead mallet wrapped in felt. The imperial physician, Dr. Kraepelin-Mayer, tapped my knee with his little nickel hammer last Tuesday and told me that the tiny vessels in the base of my brain are turning to chalk; he says the blood no longer flows *through* the grey coils, but merely pools *around* them, like canal-water backing into a clogged sewer-grate during the Scirocco. He asked me if I could still recall the name of the bridge where the timber-barges unloaded. I looked at his clean white cuffs, stiff with rice-starch, and I told him that I remembered only the number of cubic meters of lime required to seal its foundations. 

To tell him the name would have meant invoking the preposition that binds the timber to the water, the water to the pier, the pier to Julian’s chest as he leaned over the railing to catch the sounding-lead. If I speak that word, the ink in the mouth curdles. My tongue feels like a salted ox-tongue drying on a hook in a butcher’s shop in the Karst.

---

### III. THE LABYRINTH OF THE REDACTED SPANDRELS

#### 1. Lexicographical Lemma: Second Entry

**ZWIßLING** (prep., governing both the dative of petrified rest and the accusative of vanishing motion).  
*Etymology:* Derived from the obsolete Leopoldinisch adverbial formative *zwi-* (twofold, cleft) and the Illyrian-Slavic suffix *-inye* (denoting an area of marshy inundation). Eradicated from all municipal primers during the Great Orthogonal Alignment of 1894.

*   **Grammatical Category:** Spatial-temporal preposition of absolute liminality.
*   **Definition:** Designates the condition of being permanently suspended between a physical architectural threshold that has been pulverized by municipal decree and the mental anticipation of crossing that threshold to reach a person who ceased to exist prior to the utterance of the verb. Unlike *zwischen* (which presupposes two extant coordinates), *zwißling* denotes a state wherein the speaker is held fast by the non-existence of both the origin and the terminus.
*   **Condemnation Citation:** *“The use of the preposition* zwißling* in any private testamentary document, commercial bill of lading, or declaration of romantic attachment is henceforth prohibited under pain of perpetual exile to the lead-mines of Idrija. The concepts formerly conveyed by this vocable shall in all instances be replaced by the neutral copulative* und *[and], or omitted entirely through the use of an approved bureaucratic caesura.”* — *Verordnungsblatt des k.k. Justizministeriums*, Nr. 12/b, Wien, 1895.

***

#### 2. Surveyor’s Field Notes: Station 08 to 19 (The Hypogeum of St. Dismas)

```
[Level: -4.80m below Mean Adriatic High Water.
Atmospheric pressure: 778mm Hg. Carbonic acid concentration: 3.2%.
Instrument: Ertel & Sohn Reversible Level, brass-mounted.]
```

At Station 11, the brick tunnel of the former *Sotto-Portico dei Lavandai* terminates abruptly against a vertical bulkhead of uncoursed cyclopean masonry, evidently erected during the panic of the post-seismic quarantine. 

The masonry defies the elementary rules of stereotomy. The stones—irregular blocks of bituminous marl quarried from the upper Carso—do not rest upon horizontal beds; they are laid in radiating, logarithmic spirals that draw the eye toward a blind central oculum no larger than a child’s cranium. When I align the crosshairs of the Ertel level upon the central joint of the oculum, the spirit-level bubble refuses to stabilize. The glass vial, though hermetically sealed in Munich and filled with non-freezing alcohol, demonstrates an erratic, boiling agitation.

```

       |   STA. 14: BLIND ARCADE WITH LOGARITHMIC MASONRY      |
       |                                                       |
       |                 . - ~ ~ ~ - .                         |
       |             . '       |       ' .                     |

       |           \           |           /                   |
       |             . ' _ _ _ | _ _ _ ' .                     |
       |                       |                               |
       | <- [DISTANCE TO JULIAN'S TALLOW-DESK: UNRECORDABLE] ->|
       +-------------------------------------------------------+
```

The gallery beyond this wall was once the *Vicolo del Filatoio*. According to the 1888 Cadastral Survey, it contained seven silk-throwing mills, twelve tenements of four stories each, and a public fountain fed by the subterranean waters of the Timavo. 

None of these structures have been demolished in the Euclidean sense; rather, they appear to have been compressed laterally by the narrowing of the street’s cross-section. Through a fracture in the scagliola revetment, I inserted the graduated brass sounding-rod to its full length of four meters. It encountered no void, nor did it strike solid resistance; the sensation transmitted through the metal was that of thrusting a cane into a barrel of half-congealed lard or cooled tallow. 

The hygrometer now registers total saturation: drops of dense, ferruginous water fall from the ceiling at regular intervals of eleven seconds, each drop striking the surface of my vulcanized rubber boots with the distinct, dry snap of an ivory billiard-ball.

***

#### 3. Confessional Register: The Thinning of the Coordinates

Water to the calves. Bitter cold. The smell of cold fat and old lime. 

I must not say *Julian was behind the wall*. The word *behind* has been walled up by the masons from Trieste. If I say *behind*, my pencil splits down the cedar casing; if I think *behind*, the left side of my tongue goes numb, as it did three months ago while I was taking tea with the District Inspector in the café on the *Piazza Grande*. 

The Inspector was eating a plum tart. He chewed with his mouth open, his grey Austrian whiskers wet with sugar-syrup, and he spoke of the new railway terminal that will be built over the canal-rubble. He said: *The past is a swamp of bad syntax, Herr Ober-Konzipist. A city with too many small alleyways produces an irregular pulse in the lower classes. An alleyway is an uncontrolled subordinate clause; it leads the citizen into grammatical insubordination. When we have laid the iron tracks in straight lines from the North Station to the docks, the population will speak only in the indicative present.*

I dropped my spoon. I reached for the napkin, but my hand could not find the path *across* the marble table. The table was there. The napkin was there. The space was gone. 

Now, in this vault, the water climbs toward my knees. It is not *rising*; it is simply that the stone is getting shorter. The limestone dissolves under the lantern-oil. 

Julian’s face is losing its corners. He had a small brown mole under his left eyelid—the eye he squinted when he looked through the eyepiece of the level. Yesterday I tried to sketch that mole in the margins of the *Monthly Hydrological Summary*, but the pencil would only make straight, bureaucratic strokes: vertical, horizontal, zero. The curve has been forbidden. 

If I cannot draw the curve of his cheekbone, how will the light find him when the tide goes out? The water tastes of salt and iron filings. A dead rat drifts past my thigh, floating high and stiff, its belly white as a communion wafer, its tiny claws curled around a sliver of cork.

### IV. THE TERMINAL SUMP OF THE SOTTO-RIVA

#### 1. Lexicographical Lemma: Third Entry

**SPUNDWEICHE, die** (f., no plural).  
*Etymology:* Technical compound from Middle High German *spunt* (the bung of a cask; an iron-reinforced sluice-gate) and *weiche* (a yielding, a softening, a railway-switch). Originally employed exclusively by the caulkers and dry-dock overseers of the San Leopoldo Admiralty.

*   **Grammatical Category:** Nominal substantive of material and mental liquefaction.
*   **Definition:** The sudden, catastrophic loss of load-bearing rigidity in maritime masonry caused by the long-term chemical interaction of salt-spray, human grease, and the systemic suppression of the true names of the waterways flowing beneath the foundations. Characterized by the stones assuming the consistency of wet curd while retaining their outward historical coloration, so that a surveyor leaning his weight against an apparently solid pier finds his shoulder sinking into the core of the wall as though it were a vat of fermenting polenta.
*   **Condemnation Citation:** *“All instances of the term* Spundweiche *occurring in maritime insurance policies, architectural estimates, or hospital admission forms shall be excised with an iron stylus and replaced by the phrase* normaler Verschleiß *[customary wear-and-tear]. The K.k. Port Health Authority shall treat any building inspector reporting the condition as suffering from melancholic delirium.”* — *Triester Zeitung*, Beilage für das Küstenland, 21 Juni 1896.

***

#### 2. Surveyor’s Field Notes: Station 20 to Omega (The Redacted Sump)

```
[Level: Undefined. Hydrostatic head: 11.2 meters. Lantern light failing.
Theodolite tripod abandoned at Station 18 due to the liquefaction of the floor-flags.]
```

The gallery has ceased to conform to the three Cartesian axes. 

The floor does not dip; it *unfolds*. The ashlar courses of the main conduit—originally executed in the finest rusticated granite from the quarries of Nabresina—have undergone the phase-transition described in the contraband glossaries as *Spundweiche*. I tested the central pier of the third blind arch with the point of my steel-tipped timber-gauge: the metal passed through eighteen inches of dressed granite without meeting greater resistance than that offered by an over-ripe cheese. 

The masonry did not crumble; it closed behind the withdrawal of the instrument like warm sealing-wax, leaving no borehole.

The vaulting above has assumed a pentagonal groin-configuration that cannot be projected upon a flat sheet of paper by any system of descriptive geometry known to the Imperial-Royal Polytechnic Institutes. Five separate ribs spring from a single impost on the southern wall, yet they do not meet at a central boss; they loop around one another in continuous, unbroken curves, like the intestines of an eviscerated calf, disappearing into pockets of dense, black damp where the air is so heavy with saltpeter that the lantern flame burns blue and no longer than a hazelnut.

My boots are stuck fast in the pavement. The limestone has softened around the leather uppers, rising to the ankles like cold dough. 

I have unbuckled the straps and stepped out upon the naked silt. The temperature of the water is 4.5 degrees Réaumur. The transit instrument has settled into the mud at an angle of thirty-three degrees; its brass circle, calibrated in Vienna by the master mechanician Starke, is coated with a greasy film of green copper carbonate. Through the sighting-tube, I see neither level-staff nor masonry: I see only the reflection of my own left pupil, hugely magnified by the wet lens, clouded by that milky crescent which Dr. Kraepelin-Mayer called the *Arcus senilis*—the ring of lime that forms around the edge of the living eye when the brain begins to forget where it has stored the light.

***

#### 3. Confessional Register: The Terminal Parataxis

Water at the breast. 

Cold. Cold. Lime on the tongue. 

The wall is no wall. The wall is soft grease. My fingers go in. To the wrist. To the elbow. The stone eats the sleeve of my coat. The imperial cloth. Fine green wool from Reichenberg. Eaten by the stone. 

No *here*. No *there*. 

Julian. The mouth full of mud. 

Not *in* the mud. Not *under* the mud. 

Julian mud. Stone mud. Alois mud. 

The Commission has taken the little words. They took *from*. They took *to*. They took *with*. 

A man cannot weep *with* his eyes. He weeps eyes. The salt comes out of the bone. 

The lantern is dead. The wick went *twick* in the black grease. A small smell. Like a tallow candle blown out in a church after the third mass for the cholera-dead. 

My feet have no toes. Just white lard in the water. 

I reach out. The stone is not stone. It is his shoulder. No. It is the pier of the tallow-dock. No. It is the rib of the barge that went down with the eight horses and the kegs of red ochre. 

The red ochre is in the water. Everything red. Red in the mouth. Red in the dark. 

The pencil is gone. Dropped into the slit between the stones. 

Not *between*. 

Dropped slit stones. 

```
                                  *
                             .         .
                         .                 .
                       (                     )
```

The water is smooth now. High tide over the lips. 

A good tongue. A clean tongue. No words in it. 

No *Julian*. 

Just the salt. 

Just the cold Istrian lime. 

The vault is coming down. It does not drop. It leans. It touches the hair. It touches the forehead. 

Like a hand with wet tallow on the fingers. 

The surveyor stands. The level sinks. 

The city is finished. 

Zero. 

Zero. 

Zero.

#### FIELD-SURVEY NOTES: STATION 001–009 (Sector: Fondaco dei Morlacchi, Sub-level III)

*Station 001.* Azimuth 214° towards the blind groin-vaulting of the former *Sottoportico dei Canestrai*. Masonry constructed of porous Istrian calcarenite with thick beds of hydraulic pozzolana mortar. Hygrometric paper indicates 98% saturation. The salt-efflorescence (*salpetro*) has formed stalactitic crusts five centimeters thick along the intrados, distorting the profile of the transverse arches. 

*Station 002.* The leveling rod at the plinth shows an inexplicable vertical displacement. The chain measurement between the western pier and the half-buried water-gate yields 14.28 meters; yet the transit sighting reveals that the transverse arch spans only 9.10 meters without showing any structural shear or masonry buckling. The space contracts in the horizontal axis while maintaining an unyielding verticality. Plumb-bob hangs true to gravity, yet the water’s surface beneath it slopes upward toward the south-southeast at an angle of roughly three degrees. 

*Station 003.* Pendentives above the submerged arcade. The stonework is executed in a coarse diamond-point rustication (*bugnato*), though the relief seems smoothed, not by the wash of tidal silt, but by a continuous, low-frequency atmospheric vibration. When the drafting stylus is brought against the joint between the third voussoir and the keystone, the metal vibrates at a pitch corresponding to middle C (approx. 261 Hz). No water turbulence is visible in the sump-pool below. The water itself is leaden, thick with suspended coal-dust and macerated vegetable fiber.

*Station 004.* Anomaly of the blind arcade. The southern wall contains seven round-headed niches faced in imitation porphyry (*scagliola*). According to the cadastral map of 1888, this wall was the exterior party-wall of the Consorzio di Farina. However, the depth of the niches exceeds the known thickness of the adjoining quay by at least four meters. Upon thrusting the four-meter pine measuring rod into the fourth niche, the tip met no resistance; the air drawn from the aperture carries the smell of cold, slaked lime, dried bay leaves, and human hair.

***

#### CONFESSIONAL FRAGMENTS: ALOIS VANECEK

It was in the winter after the cholera, when the lagoon froze from the Lazaretto Vecchio as far as the mouth of the Isonzo, that we first noticed the thinning of the mortar in his room on the Rio dei Barcaroli. Julian said nothing. He sat at the drafting table with his fingers stained with sepia ink, his dividers poised over the vellum plan of the Arsenal, while outside the window the ice groaned against the oak pilings. 

Now, three paces into this flooded culvert, I am searching for the word that governed the space between his collarbone and the gray wool of his surveyor’s waistcoat—that small, hollow recess where the air smelled always of roasted chicory and winter rain. The Edict has removed the syllable. When I search the official *Kanzleiwörterbuch* for the preposition that denotes *resting within an angle that no longer possesses an exterior*, the page is merely a strip of gray pasteboard, glued over with official gum.

The lantern casts an oval of pale yellow grease upon the limestone. The water rises to my gaiters, cold as well-water in Styria. My left eye suffers from that dark, fibrous cobweb—the physician in Graz called it *apoplexia levis*, a softening of the cerebral vessels, a leak of dark blood into the chambers where the city was once filed away in cedar drawers. When I look at the archway before me, the voussoirs double: the stone above, the phantom below. But it is not a reflection. In the reflection, Julian’s red levelling staff is still standing against the pier, though the pier itself was dynamited five summers ago by order of the Imperial Administrator to make way for the new Customs Depot.

I can no longer say *behind*. 

If I say *behind*, the pen stumbles on the rag-paper; the hand shakes until the ink splatters like crushed elderberries. I must write: *in the condition of that which follows without distance*. I must write: *the place that remains when the walker has been excised from the pavement*.

The saltpeter tastes of bitter almond on my lower lip.

#### FIELD-SURVEY NOTES: STATION 010–022 (Sector: Rio Secco, Vault of the Icon-Carvers)

*Station 010.* Reached the lower terrace of the submerged crypt of *San Girolamo*. The structure consists of four quadripartite groin-vaults supported by monolithic columns of cipollino marble. The bases are buried under approximately 1.10 meters of black, alluvially deposited mud containing fragments of terracotta roof tiles and bone meal. 

*Station 011.* Optical transit calculation: The angle between the southwest column and the altar-stipe was recorded as 47° 12′ in my survey of October 1889. The current measurement, repeated three times with the vernier scale under the oil lamp, reads 61° 44′. Yet the distance between the plinths remains exactly 3.84 meters as measured by the steel tape. The space has widened internally without extending its exterior perimeter. The marble shaft of the northeast column shows no horizontal displacement, yet its entasis appears compressed, as if viewed through a thick layer of unrefined bottle-glass.

*Station 012.* The acoustic test. A light blow with the copper-faced mallet upon the keystone of the central bay produces a resonance of extraordinary duration. The sound does not decay exponentially; rather, it climbs through the overtone series, reaching the eleventh harmonic (G-sharp) and remaining suspended in the water-vapor for ninety-four seconds. During this period, the surface tension of the water around my thighs forms concentric hexagonal ripples (*chladnische Klangfiguren*), identical to the geometric patterns of the floor-mosaics in the church above, which were removed by the Amelioration Commission in July 1895.

*Station 013.* The hygrometer reads 100%. Condensation falls from the brick vaults not in isolated drops, but in fine, warm filaments that resemble unspun silk. My fingertips, upon touching the mortar-joints, are stained with a bright Prussian blue (*Berlinerblau*), although no pigment was ever recorded in the structural fabric of these foundations. The brickwork has begun to soften; it has the consistency of cold marzipan and can be indented with the thumb to a depth of two centimeters.

***

#### CONFESSIONAL FRAGMENTS: ALOIS VANECEK

The pencil point breaks. 

I must sharpen it with the bone-handled knife, but the shavings do not fall into the water. They float upward, like small brown moths, and adhere to the wet vault above my head. My eyes—the left one is now almost entirely filled with that dark, pulsating jelly—see the room as it was when we laid out the sheets of tracing linen over the marble flags of the sacristy. Julian wore that ring with the carnelian intaglio—a head of Antinous, worn smooth by his thumb. When he dipped the brush into the gum water, his sleeve caught the corner of my drafting board. 

The Commission has forbidden the word for the sound of silk when it brushes against damp pine. They have named it: *Geräuschlosigkeit* (Class IV, Category C). 

Now, when I try to remember the way he turned toward the doorway when the bells of the Jesuits rang five o'clock across the canal, I find only the official vacancy. The sentence has no middle. There is only: *Julian* and then the white gap, four inches of blank rag-paper, and then *the water beneath the timber floor*.

He was not drowned. He did not die in the collapse of the quay. He was simply *redigiert*—struck through with the two parallel red-chalk lines that we used in the cartographic bureau to signify a sewer-channel that had been filled with gravel. His name was taken from the parish register at San Niccolò, his tax assessments were distributed among three non-existent tanners in the Strada Nuova, and his drafting tools—the silver-plated proportional compasses, the bone scale, the English ink-stones—were auctioned as *unclaimed imperial chattels*.

I bought the compasses. I have them in my waistcoat pocket now. The steel point is rusted into its sleeve. It presses against my seventh rib like a cold tooth.

How does one say: *the room into which someone will never again return, though his shadow remains dried into the lime of the northern wall*? 

The new lexicon offers: *Leerstand* (n.m., bureaucratic). A term for empty warehouses. It does not contain the cold tallow. It does not contain the particular gray green of his eyes when the sea-fog rolled in from the breakwater.

My left leg is cold. The wool is heavy. It smells of river-mud and sheep-fat. The water is at my groin.

```
      │             │             │             │
```

#### FIELD-SURVEY NOTES: STATION 023–FINIS (Sector: Unknown; triangulation lost)

*Station 023.* The compass needle is erratic. It spins smoothly through 360 degrees without settling, then dips vertically toward the floor of the vault. I have dropped the steel chain; it cannot be recovered from the silt. The water is no longer cold; it has reached the temperature of blood drawn from a horse’s neck (approx. 37.5° C).

*Station 024.* Description of the masonry: There are no longer any headers or stretchers (*Köpfe und Läufer*). The wall is composed of a continuous, dense, gray matter that resembles calcified brain tissue or the compressed ledgers of the Municipal Tax Office. When the fingernail is pressed into the surface, it leaves a white groove from which a thin, milky fluid exudes, smelling of vinegar and damp linen.

*Station 025.* The arch above me is neither Roman nor pointed; it is a catenary formed by the sagging of the ceiling under the weight of the city above. Through the fissures in the brick, I hear the iron wheels of the morning milk-carts crossing the *Piazza Giuseppina*. The sounds are muffled, as if filtered through twenty cubits of river-sand. The distance between the pavement above and the water below is no more than five feet, yet the sounding-lead, when dropped into the gap between my boots, sinks twelve fathoms without striking the rock bottom of the lagoon.

*Station 026.* The survey is complete. The angles sum to zero. The four walls of the crypt are parallel, yet they meet at four right angles and enclose nothing. The drawing pen no longer leaves an ink line; it plows a shallow furrow in the calfskin page, which immediately fills with dark, venous fluid from my thumb.

***

#### CONFESSIONAL FRAGMENTS: ALOIS VANECEK

The water is at my neck. 

No words left for *under*. No words left for *open*. 

Stone here. 
Wet here. 
Dark here.

Julian his coat. The smell of wool when the tea boiled on the spirit lamp. I cannot write *lamp*. I cannot write *tea*. 

The grease. The yellow fat of the candle in my mouth. 

I touch the corner where the brick ends and his shoulder was. The lime is soft. It yields like bread. My hand goes into the wall up to the wrist. There is no iron inside. There is no rubble. There is only the cool, wet hair of all the draftsmen who died in the year of the Great Redaction.

We were five. We were four. We were two. 

Now the page is wet. The calfskin is heavy as a drowned cat. 

I must hold the lantern with my teeth. The brass is bitter. The oil burns the tongue. 

Not *behind* the church. Not *between* the pilings. 

The state says: *There is only the line.* The line that runs from the station to the harbor. Straight. Ninety degrees. No corners where a boy can wait with his drawing-board under his arm while the rain falls on his wool cap. No vowels for the sound of his boots on the green weed of the low-tide steps.

My head is full of gray lime. 

The left eye is dark now. A black disc, like the seal on an imperial decree. 

Julian. 

The water enters the ear. It sounds like the library at Graz when the old folios are turned in the winter afternoon. The sound of dry paper. The sound of sheepskin. The sound of the Emperor’s clerks scraping the names off the parchment with their curved steel knives.

A small scrape. 
A white powder on the sleeve. 
Then nothing.

### THE PALIMPSEST OF THE CARTOGRAPHER-GENERAL
*Being an Extract from the Dossiers of the Archivium Topologicum, Veridiana, Winter 1888*
*Authored by Dr. Alistair Finch, Chief Orthographer*

---

### MOVEMENT I: THE MORPHOLOGY OF THE GRID

```
[REGISTER ENTRY: ARCHIVIUM TOPOLOGICUM // REF: 888-IV-ST.JUDE]
INSTRUMENTATION EMPLOYED: Troughton & Simms 12-inch Transit Theodolite (Brass No. 407); Vernier Calipers in Oxidized Steel; Lead-weighted Zinc Survey Plates.
SURVEYOR: Dr. A. Finch, Chief Orthographer.
OPERATIONAL OBJECTIVE: Complete eradication of the St. Jude Deflectivity; realignment of the southern quadrant along the Cartesian meridian 45°12′08″ N.
```

It is a well-established axiom of municipal sanitation that an unpunctuated street is a nursery for sedition. Where the syntax of an alleyway is permitted to waver—where a cobblestone thoroughfare curls back upon its own tail like an ill-formed *g'* or founders in the obscure, guttural diphthongs of the illiterate—the stone itself loses its structural resolve.

This morning, at precisely twenty minutes past seven, the fog over the St. Jude Quarter possessed the exact, sickly density of unrefined mutton tallow. I stood upon the parapet of the Old Granary with the brass housing of the Troughton & Simms transit press’d cold against my right cheekbone. Through the reticle’s crossed spider-webs, I observed the corner of *Gasse-den-Blinden*.

Or rather, what remained of it.

Thirty years ago, before the enactment of the *Edict of Municipal Lexicography (Imperial Decree No. 14)*, the *Gasse* did not terminate at the river wall as logic dictates. It folded inward upon its own genitive declensions. A traveler descending its western slope would enter a cobbler’s shop at No. 14, step through the rear vestibule to fetch his boots, and emerge—without having altered his compass heading by a single arc-second—into the high courtyard of the Ottoman Customs House three miles to the east. This spatial hemiplegia was not a miracle; it was merely the consequence of the local population insisted upon calling the thoroughfare *Vör-Zelath*, a noun whose archaic locative case demanded a double-folded horizon.

I turned the fine micro-metric adjustment screw of the theodolite three threads to the right. The crosshairs bisected the lintel of an old weaver’s cottage.

"Read the azimuth, Mr. Haffner," I said without turning.

Behind me, the ink froze in the nib of my assistant’s pen with a faint, crystalline snap.

"Three hundred degrees, eleven minutes, sir," Haffner murmured, his coat collar turned up against the damp sulfur mist rising from the coal barges. "Though... if I may venture, Dr. Finch... the zinc plate from the 1858 ordinance reads three hundred and fourteen."

"The 1858 ordinance was transcribed in the *Vör-dialect*," I replied, my voice dry as dried elderberries. "It was drafted by men who believed that stone possessed a memory independent of the Emperor’s vocabulary. The four minutes of arc you find missing have not been lost, Haffner. They have been erased. We have excised the lingering subjunctive from the granite."

I stepped back from the instrument and pulled my sheepskin-lined gloves tight across my knuckles. Beneath us, in the narrow gorge of the quarter, the workmen of the Eighth Mechanical Corps were already driving the iron surveyors' stakes into the moist basalt. With every blow of the sixteen-pound sledgehammers, a dry, sharp ring echoed through the gorge—not the dull *thud* of metal striking rock, but a high, singing frequency, like glass under a glazier’s diamond.

Where the hammer fell upon stone that had been successfully purged of its vernacular names, the earth remained stable, grey, and rectilinear. But twenty yards to the north, where the old women of the quarter still whispered their morning prayers in the banned dialect of the *Alt-Veridian*, the masonry writhed under the iron. I saw through my glass how a brick chimney on the *Bäckerstrasse* shuddered with a grotesque, peristaltic ripple, its lime-mortar weeping yellow moisture as if trying to re-form the soft, rounded vowels of a language that no longer possessed an official alphabet.

It is a agonizing business, this cartographic hygiene. 

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| MARGINALIA: FINCH (PERMUTATION OBSERVED AT 08:45 AM)                     |
| The right wall of the Registry Office exhibits a drift of 0.04 feet per  |
| diem toward the north-west. This coincides precisely with my removal of  |
| the noun 'Die Stille-vor-dem-Klopfen' from the Municipal Dictionary.     |
| Query: Does the stone drift because the word is dead, or because I am    |
| the only one left who remembers how to spell it?                        |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

My hands are no longer steady when I handle the brass calipers. For three weeks—ever since the telegram arrived from the provincial sanatorium at Ostrig, bearing the official stamp of the mortuary registrar—my left eye has been afflicted with a subtle scotoma. When I look directly at a straight line, whether it be the plumb-bob wire hanging from the tripod or the printed margin of my own ledger, the center of the line appears to sag. It curves downward into a shallow, dark ellipse, shaped suspiciously like the accent mark used in the old *Veridian* dative of bereavement.

Clara died on the fourteenth of November. Or so the telegram claimed.

Yet, when I consult the *Gazetteer of the Outer Enclaves* which I compiled between the years 1862 and 1870, the town of Ostrig does not appear on page 412 where I know I set its bearings. In its place is a blank square of vellum, yellowed at the margins, marked only with the dry, powdery residue of an ink-eraser.

Did I ban the village before or after she moved there?

I reached into my breast pocket and felt the stiff, folded edge of her final letter. It had arrived unsealed, written upon thin, oily butcher's paper. It was not composed in the clear, copperplate hand I had forced her to practice during her childhood in the Archivium's nursery—that crisp, Cartesian script designed to cultivate spatial obedience. No; she had written it in the wild, dense, heavily inflected runes of her mother’s family. It was a text bristling with double-hooked sibilants, triple-dotted vowels, and locative suffixes that have not been pronounced inside the city walls since the winter of the Great Orthographic Cleansing.

"Dr. Finch?" Haffner was watching me. His young face was pinched with cold, his nose red above his woolen scarf. "The team at the base of the aqueduct needs the target vector for the new abattoir. If we do not set the datum line before noon, the masonry will settle into the old creekbed."

"The old creekbed no longer exists, Mr. Haffner," I said, stepping back to the theodolite. "I struck it from the hydrology register in '74. It is now a line of zero elevation."

I leaned over the glass. But as I adjusted the objective lens, the crosshairs did not reveal the clean, vertical line of the red-painted survey pole. Instead, I saw a narrow, spiraling staircase of dark schist, winding down into a fog so thick it appeared to have been carved out of damp chalk. At the head of the stairs stood a child, her back turned to me, wearing a pinafore of faded indigo print—a print whose pattern was formed entirely of repeating, interlocking letters from an alphabet I burnt thirty years ago.

I closed my left eye. The vision remained. I closed my right. The vision grew clearer.

---

### MOVEMENT II: THE LEXICON OF THE BANNED VERNACULAR

To understand the necessity of our labors—and the sheer, terrifying elasticity of the ground upon which Veridiana is built—the scholar must first divest himself of the vulgar error that stone is an immutable substance. Stone is merely a heavy, slow noun. If a community speaks of a wall for five hundred years as *Die Muer*, the granite retains a certain dry, brittle density corresponding to the short vowel and the hard, unyielding alveolar stop. But if that same wall is named in the vernacular *Sørvane*, it ceases to act as a barrier and becomes a semi-permeable linguistic membrane.

Here follow three lexicographical entries extracted from my private *Index Librorum Prohibitorum* (Archivium Topologicum, Secret Cabinet VII):

